confidence_note: The reference TR text's title calls compounding 'the most powerful force of the free market' and invokes a quote often attributed to Einstein about compound interest; that attribution is widely considered apocryphal and is not used. Robbins's book strongly emphasizes compounding and the importance of starting early. To illustrate the principle, the story uses a classic hypothetical comparison of an early saver and a late saver; it is presented as an illustration of Robbins's point, not as a specific example from the book, since its exact form in the book cannot be confirmed. The numbers in the illustration are round and approximate, using an assumed steady return.
facts: Robbins argues that compounding, returns earning further returns over time, is the key force that turns modest savings into significant wealth.
He stresses that time is the most important ingredient: the earlier you start, the more years compounding has to work.

A classic illustration: one person invests a fixed amount each year from about age 19 to 27 and then stops; another starts at 27 and invests the same yearly amount until 65. With a steady high return, the early starter can end up with a comparable or even larger sum despite contributing for far fewer years.
The exact result depends on the assumed rate of return; the pattern, that early years are extremely valuable, holds across reasonable assumptions.
Robbins's message: don't wait until you earn more to start; start with what you have, and let time work.
Real returns vary year to year; illustrations use steady averages for simplicity.
tension: Waiting until you earn more seems sensible. Compounding makes waiting expensive.
opening_idea: Two friends save the same amount each year. One starts at 19 and stops at 27. The other starts at 27 and never stops. Guess who ends up with more.

lessons.idea: Early years are the most valuable.
